outcome.why: A communication rule about how replies should be written, not a build or doc item.

Give an overview of the data structure.
When and where is a session record created?
When and where is it saved?

How does a session differ from a task regarding directories?
Does task.jsonl go right into the session folder?

outcome.why: The reply explained the session and task classes, their data and where they are saved.

parts.text: Minions write everything to their own session log instead of replying to the mastermind via chat, and keep that log up to date.
Is there a tail system yet for agents to watch session or task logs? I don't think so, but maybe it exists.
Any mastermind could tail any log, so agents can talk through logs; agent-to-agent talk is not bad, and I think I asked for this before.
Chat leaves no paper trail, so core work goes in logs; quick clarifications via chat are fine.
Reasonable-size work, like starting an investigation, gets an overview in the session log, and could even be a task.
Investigating probably does not need a new file.
Maybe a new task gets created within the session log so we can track what is currently open.
The mastermind subscribes to its minion's session log, so it reacts the moment the minion writes an update; small tasks can just write to the session log.
The session log does not need much detail; it should be an overview of what is being worked on.

outcome.why: The messaging doc records that minions report by logging to their session and chat is for clarifications.

parts.text: Module documentation goes directly into the module's README or docs, never buried in session directories; when possible, work on the official documentation.

outcome.why: The owner doc records that module documentation goes in the module's own readme or docs.

outcome.why: A worry the owner raised, not a request to build anything.

add.subject: Figma design of session and task views

parts.text: Don't wait on me for decisions; figure out what I haven't said yet and keep everything moving.

outcome.why: The rule to decide without waiting is recorded in the owner's memory index as 'No parking on approval'; it is a behaviour rule, not a repo change.

parts.text: Stay under pace and watch tokens: don't do more than we need.

outcome.why: The design-first doc line 7 records 'Stay under pace; do no more than needed.'

parts.text: Dictation feature is wanted but not top priority.

outcome.why: Line 7 records that dictation matters but is not top priority, so nothing was built for it.

parts.text: Design session and task views in Figma first: make a new page for session and task work and design card previews for the single session detail page and the single task page.
Can you create a new Figma document, or only use existing ones? I don't believe you can make a new file.
Work in the September 2026 Figma doc (logged under ext/Figma, maybe); create new pages there, not new files.
Task cards need to show content, subtasks, and a progress bar.
Design month and day views with multiple card sizes (single row, or multi-row data grid); cards show the most useful info and are mobile friendly; the day view is a list of session cards.
Session cards should have proper titles and an overview of the session, e.g. three main tasks shown checked off.
Preview content could vary by session; maybe hide previews and show only names to see more at once.

Explore the design space in Figma: multiple sizes from 400px up to 1,000-2,000px, multi-column layouts for browsing any scope (month, year, day), and lists of matching sessions or tasks, plus a single session page.
The single session page could have tabs: a chat tab for the messages and an overview tab for status, cost, and details.
Owner is thinking through the different views and what would be useful; no action requested.

outcome.why: A new 'Sessions and tasks' page with session, task and project card frames was built in the owner's September Figma file.

parts.text: Design before building: explore and test the views in Figma first, adjust what doesn't work, finalize, and only then build them in the browser so we know exactly what we're getting; don't go down the view-class rabbit hole yet.

outcome.why: The doc sets the order: explore and approve the views in Figma before any browser build, and the build itself stays unstarted.

parts.text: The inbox, session system, and preview rail opening columns that open more columns may have been a mistake to attempt, since the goal wasn't described clearly yet.

outcome.why: Line 27 records the owner's note that the preview-rail column idea may have been a mistake, with no action taken.

parts.text: Lists render each item's preview, never the full detail; the preview rail is the list.

outcome.why: Line 27 states that lists behave like the preview rail: preview in the list, full render on its own page.

parts.text: Where is the session class stored, and should the preview and full session views be methods on session, a session view class with versions, or plain render/preview template functions? Owner wants to discuss this before deciding.

outcome.why: Line 23 lists the class-versus-template options for the owner to discuss, and the decision is left open.

parts.text: Progress bar should be one generalized component with types, appearances, and segment data inputs; build reusable pieces as much as possible.

outcome.why: Line 19 specifies one generalized progress bar with segments, composites, appearances and one data input, and the Figma anatomy frame covers it.

parts.text: Owner agrees the Figma-first approach makes sense.
Session and task views are the top priority; write that down.

outcome.why: Line 7 states that the session and task views are the top priority, and the doc was committed.

parts.text: Make subscriptions universal for any item through one generic subscribe in the store, rather than only the JSONL tail; work out whether that means JSONL tail or cloud pub/sub.
The store could handle the socket plumbing.
Owner is unsure how the current socket/tail streaming works.

outcome.why: Line 11 states that subscribe is universal through the store, but the design is not built yet.

parts.text: Make items nest: an item can hold child items, and work out the nesting rules and storage that come with it.
Maybe list extends item.
It gets really complicated.
Can an item have items?
Should an item have items?
An item's items list should be created on demand, not on every item.
Once an item gets a child it becomes a node or folder.
Default: dropping one item onto another acts as an inbox; this is a good default.
Nesting structure and storage have a few options.
Storage options for a nested item: inside the parent's JSONL, its own storage, a .js file exporting the instance, dynamically created JSONL, plain JSON, or a DB.
Has the event-driven list idea, using lists to save for persistence, actually been implemented?
Automatically wire the storage mechanism when one item is added to another.
Owner is unsure the best way to handle storage, since the history was snapshots.
We used to snapshot whole state on change; now we use deltas that can replay state, and we think that works.
Pages use either an existing JSONL or dynamic pages; most things use JSONL storage for now, which is fine.
Configure the storage file name per item type, with some level of configuration for items.
Sessions save into a dated session JSONL file, which matches and is good.
Once an item exists, other items can be dragged and dropped onto it.
For a session, anything added may by default become embedded.
Give an overview of session: does Session extend Item?
A session could have its own items list.
Content may be the same thing as the items list, just a list that shows which items are in it.
Showing child items by default is probably useful.
Content could be a template system where anything can be written and child items can be embedded.
An item is a universal file/folder/page object that can be upgraded to a page, and adding items across storage forms raises a decision.
Adding one item to another generally leaves the item where it lives, as a reference, not a move.
A move mode, or a modifier key like control or shift, triggers the actual move.
A move removes the item from its current location, such as a parent JSONL into its own JSONL or its own directory.
There are different storage targets and the store probably has different mechanisms for them.
Persisting to a .js file is hard without rewriting the file, so not all items have easy persistence.
A .js item could persist through a cloud API or local storage, so being a JS file does not preclude persistence.
Owner has stopped caring about the code API and naming, since the agent writes it.
Show how storage is configured and what the user experience looks like on screen.
How does the user know where things live, and do they even care?
Owner needs to understand where things live: use a different visual representation per storage mode, or a field noting the storage mechanism.
Wire everything recursively: when an item gets children it automatically gets persistence, and sub-items do the same, so drag and drop wires storage up correctly.

outcome.why: The doc lays out items held on demand, reference-by-default adds and recursive wiring; parent-saves-child was built and tested, and the rest is still a plan.

Maybe a request and response ID is needed to match them up.
Reading the file system is pretty much synchronous.
Tools might be defined as synchronous or asynchronous, and synchronous ones should be fast.
An asynchronous tool is a synchronous request plus a queued later response.
Wrap each message so the AI knows where it came from.

parts.text: Does the SDK's page fetch just return raw HTML, or does it render client-side pages in a browser session?

outcome.why: The SDK facts doc records what the Agent SDK can do, and the probe results are filed there.

parts.text: Cloudflare is probably rendering pages in a browser session, which is why the owner is asking.

outcome.why: The reply said Cloudflare's Browser Rendering is a real browser and is the alternative for JavaScript pages.

parts.text: Write down the Anthropic/Claude SDK web page fetch as an alternative to Cloudflare.
If it works as well or better and costs only a few pennies per search, maybe use it instead.

outcome.why: The SDK doc records the plain WebFetch alternative and the cost.

parts.text: Not sure the Cloudflare versus SDK distinction matters.
Using the item tool for improvements is closely related to the JSONL data system and its deltas.

outcome.why: The item doc links the item tool to the JSONL delta system.

parts.text: Use the item tool for improvements so agents document suggestions where they will be found and they accumulate.
A recommendation that keeps surfacing gains weight and could be considered more.
Improvements in a markdown file are not easily renderable, and rendering the whole file loses per-improvement control.
Structured per-improvement records may be better, and the owner likes that idea.
Build a system for improvements at any path.
That would need another JSONL file, unless it goes into a different file.
Add a way to load the improvements.
This is exactly what is already being done with sessions and tasks.

outcome.why: The readme-system doc says improvements are one improvements.jsonl per folder, written by the item tool, with repeats adding weight.

parts.text: Tasks and/or projects should be movable to a specific path; the owner sees no reason they couldn't be.

outcome.why: The task notes state that tasks and projects can move to a module path on approval.

parts.text: Keep these artifacts as portable as possible, whether a JSONL file or a whole data directory.

outcome.why: I found no doc stating the portability principle for JSONL files and data directories.

parts.text: Mock up tasks and projects in the session directory, then on approval move them to the proper module path directory so future agents see past work.
Maybe only projects get this movement, like tasks; tasks could have that logic built in too.
The owner is not sure how they feel about that either way.

outcome.why: The task notes say a task drafts in its session folder and moves to its module tasks folder on approval.

parts.text: That makes sense.
Where do tasks and projects live on the file system? Should there be a per-path tasks subdirectory? What does the agent think?

outcome.why: The reply explained where tasks and projects live and recommended a per-path tasks folder.

parts.text: Put a per-path tasks subdirectory in place, with projects going in there.
It follows the object-oriented hierarchy.
Putting a project in a tasks directory feels a little off, but since a project is a task it works better, and there is no need for a separate projects directory.
This could work if everything flows properly, but the owner is unsure about building a robust system without misconfiguration.

outcome.why: The task notes say projects go in the same per-module tasks folder.

parts.text: Don't wait on the owner to finalize anything; try to get things done.

outcome.why: I found no written rule that agents should not wait on the owner, only the behaviour.

parts.text: Keep an eye on usage.

outcome.why: The reply reported usage as 3% of the week used against 13% of the week gone, and set a pace trigger.

parts.text: Has the weekly reset already happened, given it was Wednesday at 10 p.m.?

outcome.why: a question about that moment; the session moved on, so it needs no answer now (prompt audit, 2026-10-23)

parts.text: Did the owner really not do anything yesterday?

outcome.why: a question about that moment; the session moved on, so it needs no answer now (prompt audit, 2026-10-23)

parts.text: Be the autonomous mastermind: keep things moving, get it done, approve processes yourself, and build a planning process.
Think through process types: not every quick fix needs a whole process, and simple tasks stay simple.
Investigation tasks check something (look into this or that); their result may trigger a process refinement.
Process refinement is built into the process; tasks can be removed from it when deemed unnecessary.
What API and logic does the node loop need to check in on processes and make sure they finish properly?
The goal is to complete sessions: every task, project, process and item in a session must be checked off before moving on; abandoned items are deactivated and no longer affect completion.
Should a project be a process, extend a process, or have a process, given that a project started as a task and movement should stick to projects?

outcome.why: The autonomous mastermind built and merged the process system, and approved its own merges.

parts.text: Design sessions, projects, tasks and processes in Figma first, on a new page in the September 2026 file, then approve and implement.
Create the new page, but find the old sessions and tasks page that already has designed content.
Build robust mobile-first layouts that surface the most important information; the mobile to desktop multi-column view is its own process.
Sessions should show the most important data from session.jsonl, such as cost and model.
Browse by year, month or day to see an index of only the sessions for that day.
Within a session, create projects and tasks; when approved they can be moved to...
At some point I may want a closer eye; link me to the UI for sessions, projects and tasks.
The session page shows open tasks with status and open and closed counts, lets me click through any task or project, and structures content within each session and task.
Experiment with designs where any card can hold arbitrary content, including a rendered list of tasks.
Maybe content uses a template tag to reference the list, so arbitrary content can sit above or below it or filter it.
Alternative: a content box and a separate subtask box, with content first, maybe a short paragraph.
What content does a task need, can a question be added to a task, should a question extend task, and should a task stay incomplete until its question is answered?
Spawn a Figma agent.
ext/Figma should be documented in the framework README.
When doing Figma work, load the ext/Figma documentation, the README, and potentially sub-READMEs.
Use an Opus agent for the Figma designer, because we want to do this properly.
The Figma mastermind can launch its own agents and maybe explore the design space in parallel.
The Figma mastermind considers the overall workflow and can ask the system architect for a quick synopsis or a specific question.
The Figma agent should read the main readmes to understand the task and session system architecture.
Detail views matter most; route each item so links work and survive a refresh.
Some sessions page and Figma design work may already exist.
Standard procedure for building any widget: design in Figma first, review and improve, approve, then implement.
Experiment with different card designs.
Use mobile-width frames, not device frames or cropped header and footer frames, so long scrollable and arbitrary content fits.
Group variants into masonry-style sections of three columns, or four or five, with roughly equal column heights.
Can Figma's grid tool or wrapping flex produce masonry columns, and does flex ordering work for that?
Explore color variations by duplicating the master component and changing its color scheme.
The background color is not part of the color scheme; set it manually, and the text theme follows whether the background is light.
Use Figma responsive settings so tokens adapt at different resolutions.
How should a mobile card have a header and footer?
Explore card types: full-width edge-to-edge header, padded content area, and minimal-padding card, without wasting horizontal space on a narrow phone, including nesting and sub-cards.
Try wrapper mode: the root card has no padding or gap, and the header, main and footer each own their padding, full width with zero gap; play with nesting.
Don't overly nest things on mobile.
Use a light gray background with white rounded cards so scrolling shows each card's edges; vertical spacing between cards can vary.
Explore data grids rendering sessions and tasks, nested subtasks, and click-through; the depth of recursive rendering is still unclear.

outcome.why: The Projects, sessions, tasks, processes page was built in Figma in the September 2026 file, with seven bands of phone-width frames.

parts.text: Keep an identified system architect that always exists, is respawned daily, and is reached through logs rather than chat.
Have a system architect available and identified so requests and questions can be passed along.
Use the send message tool to look up current sessions and find the architect's ID, or tell it there is a system architect that knows how the AI system works.
The system architect should always be spawned; the mastermind skill should say you are not the system architect and spawn one if none exists.
Respawn the system architect with fresh context about daily so it never loses context and piled-up sessions stay small.
The system architect logs everything to its own session file, identified as the system architect, so a new mastermind can get its session ID quickly.
Investigate auto compaction: check whether the SDK manages the context window and has a setting, and avoid compacting mid-task and losing needed context.
Send requests to the system architect through a log file it watches or tails, have it respond to the specific JSONL item, and subscribe so responses come through automatically.
Talk to the system architect about these communication mechanisms.
Prefer logs over chat: send agent message is handy but not logged and loses context; use a clear, concise, authoritative, queryable log that shows up in the views when it suffices.

outcome.why: The mastermind role doc says a standing system architect is spawned and reached through the logs.

add.subject: Servex keeps one live session per file

parts.text: What do you mean the Servex keeps one live session per file and updates it as each line is written?

outcome.why: The reply explained the one-live-session-per-file idea and listed the open questions.

parts.text: Any item whose store is a JSONL tail gets real-time updates: the client subscribes to server updates, and each append from an agent or Git ships instantly as a reliable feed. The server-side side of this is unclear to the owner.
Can a server-side instance subscribe to the same file requests or file changes?
The server could use a different mechanism: in the same process, update the server instance when the watcher sees a change, instead of the watcher doing the socket push.
If no server instance exists, should one be instantiated automatically? Owner is unsure.
Instantiating first might simplify the code pathways.
Owner has not looked at the code and is not familiar with how the delta processing is set up.

If the server instantiates items (leaning that way for certain things), keep server instances always synchronized with the client and the file system, and study the flow so instances update when files change.
That is probably how the socket should work.

outcome.why: The items doc records that JSONL tail changes push live to subscribers, with the design answer in one-stream.md.

parts.text: Build an item system where items can have items and live in their own file or inside another file, with granular recursive subscriptions to specific items.
Rethink how server events flow, to simplify it and make sure everything updates properly.

outcome.why: The doc states the recursive granular subscription requirement for items inside their own or a parent's file, but the nested-items build is not done.

parts.text: AI agents watch items through the same system: the item tool lets an agent subscribe to any item, path, or sub item as an SDK tool, and the subscribed deltas get queued to the agent.
Owner flags one caveat worth noting.
Raw deltas from tailing a JSONL file might be good, since agents might understand them.
Piecewise deltas on an ongoing document cause context drift, so a mastermind coordinating many tasks would get confused about what goes with what.

Maybe a filter process passes only certain items from the raw log, renders them markdown-friendly, and queues and injects them. If an item changes, maybe patch in the whole revised item instead of the delta, so the agent has full context.
Leave the delta-to-agent format for the agents to figure out.

outcome.why: The doc says agents subscribe through the item tool and get the item's current state, not raw deltas.

parts.text: Use one streaming system for the AIs, the UI, and Node, so everything flows properly and data can be queried anywhere and is accurate.

outcome.why: The doc's 'One stream for the UI, node and the agents' section records the single-streaming-system rule.

parts.text: Back to inter-agent communication.
For now chat is fine, but when possible pass things along via the file system, using the item tool to create JSONL. That is the structured content approach wanted.

outcome.why: The doc says inter-agent chat is fine for now and structured items come later.

parts.text: The UI and code for items and nested items is not there yet; that could be another project, maybe kept on the back burner until these other things are finished.

outcome.why: The doc states the full nested-items project is on the back burner, as the owner asked.

parts.text: Design the session view, maybe with multiple designs.
There is not necessarily one great design, so multiple designs may be better.
Screenshots from Figma can be read and fixed fairly easily.
The Figma mastermind should develop a process: design, review screenshots, then convert approved designs into framework code so they can be clicked through on a phone.
Browsing variants on a phone is wanted; exploring variants is a sophisticated UI the owner has thought about.
Figma's variant switcher dropdown is an example.
Templates probably need a tree: a default version, subversions, and each version is a set of deltas that could be mixed and matched if modular.
The Figma agent could mock some of these variants out, though the full design system is not needed right now.
Create clean session detail pages that show a summary of all outstanding tasks that need to be completed.

outcome.why: The Figma session-page designs A to E and the picked design B are written in mobile-cards.md.

parts.text: Get back to a full-screen mobile app, or at least let the user hide the mobile header, without breaking scrolling.
The framework's top tabs are a little broken.
The mobile navigation is fine, and the sticky header could maybe scroll away.
A scroll-away, non-sticky header is common on websites and acceptable to the owner, even just at the top.
A non-sticky header would give much more screen space.
A full-screen app breaks scrolling, and the owner is not sure how to feel about the header or what to do about it.
The owner thinks there is a way to do this but does not remember exactly how the framework does it.

outcome.why: mobile-cards.md lists the scroll-away header and full-screen options for the session page, but no code hides the header yet.

parts.text: Keep the segmented progress bars: one segment per task, green when completed, flashing orange or yellow when in progress, and red when failed, stalled, or blocked.
A segment can be made up of sub-segments.
Nesting got wonky: a 12-step process was squeezed into a tiny segment bar and was far too small.
Look at past designs and have the Figma agent produce nice clean UI that helps manage these projects.

outcome.why: mobile-cards.md records the owner's bar rule: green done, amber in progress, red stalled or blocked, one segment per child up to 12.

parts.text: Use casual chat messages only for quick information, not when the question should be a whole task.

outcome.why: The resolution doc's question row says where a question's answer goes, on the reply or a card, which is the chat-versus-task split.

parts.text: A lot of quick questions are a sign that the thing was not documented properly.

outcome.why: An observation about quick questions signalling missing docs; no doc or task took it up as its own item.

parts.text: A question could be turned into a task that answers it, while also documenting it.

outcome.why: The prompt-records brief covers turning a question into an outcome that is a task or a doc note.

parts.text: Any agent should automatically update the documentation to reflect questions like these.

outcome.why: Prompt-records gives doc-note as an outcome, but automatic doc updates for questions are not yet built.

parts.text: Make task workflows visible: each session should have embeddable tasks, and we should be able to see them getting completed.
Any one task can have its own page.
That task page could live within the parent, and both options should be explored.
An embedded task could be upgraded to a path-based task when it needs a directory, or it could just be its own file.
There are three layers, starting with a session.jsonl that could have tasks embedded.
Each task could get its own task-name.jsonl file, but once it is broken out to a file you might as well make it a directory.
A task-name/task.jsonl would then be a task directory, which gets confusing.
Any task or card can have subtasks, and you could add subtasks to it.
Detail pages should be mobile-friendly, letting the user click through any task to its subtask page and drill down.
The parent page shows a task preview, and the task detail page renders the full view if the task is composed of smaller pieces.
The preview could summarize subtasks with segmented bars and either click through or expand in place, though the differentiation is tricky.
As the owner dictates more, the owner should see these tasks come to life.
The owner might want to upgrade a task to a project.
It is not clear how the upgrade delta works; it could maybe just change the type field.
On replay, changing a child item's class may not cause it to be reinstantiated, which is a tricky architecture question.
The owner is not very familiar with instantiating from deltas and nested items, having used a snapshot system before.

outcome.why: Session tasks show on the session page, but embeddable task workflows and visible completion are still the architect's open work.

parts.text: Work autonomously, coordinate, and get as much done as possible.
Work with the system architect and the Figma mastermind, and hopefully get the process system set up.

outcome.why: A general instruction to work autonomously, not a deliverable of its own.

add.subject: mastermind skill system ported over properly

parts.text: Have the system architect review the task and session systems and the new projects and process systems in terms of skills, which are now directory-based.

outcome.why: The architect's child task covers reviewing the skills-to-directory move and the new projects and processes.

parts.text: Verify that the mastermind skill system ported over properly.
Talk to the current Figma agent and confirm it read the mastermind skill, whose location is now unclear.
Document where the mastermind skill lives. The exact location matters less than having it documented.

outcome.why: The Figma designer found the mastermind skill read wrongly, and that is now in the architect's review.

parts.text: Systematize the mechanism that launches agents as much as possible.
When a mastermind spawns an agent, it should use a named mastermind template that works like the skill.
Have the system architect work out the right way to frame these, such as session configuration or process, depending on what the session is doing.
Each session has a role-based template that handles the skill, the prompting, and the process.
The model may or may not be included in the session template, and additional instructions could be added to it.
Unsure exactly how to frame all of this.

outcome.why: The architect's task includes spawn templates (role, process, model, instructions) for launching agents.

parts.text: Systems should be well documented and clear. Do not build many moving parts that are half-linked, poorly used, or out of date.

outcome.why: The principle was passed to the architect's review; no doc records it as a standing rule of its own.

parts.text: Prioritize getting tasks onto the session page first. A major build is not needed yet.
Each session page turns its prompt into new tasks.
Tasks can be organized, upgraded to projects, and moved to specific modules once approved.
This should happen in real time, as has always been the objective.

outcome.why: The prompt-to-tasks feature was merged and shows live tasks on the session page.

parts.text: Once these prompts are sent, ask the system architect to look into the prompt refinement system.
The owner does not remember where the prompt refinement system lives.

outcome.why: The prompt mastermind's brief covers reviewing the prompt refinement system.

parts.text: Look into the prompt audit done recently and report how useful, accurate, and detailed it was.
A recent prompt audit was a rough pass: read the raw prompts and see what was asked and what was done.
The audit seemed to find a number of loose ends.
The owner does not trust how the audit happened and hardly believes it was done properly.
What confidence level or outcomes did the audit produce?
With about 3 pages of content, was the audit able to accurately extract all the asks?
When an ask did not become a task, did it become a documentation check?
Was each ask written down somewhere?
The owner's intention was that unactioned asks become documentation checks.
Did an Opus agent find more detail than a Haiku agent on the same prompt, since Haiku may struggle with large chunks?
Can Haiku process a large chunk well, or not?

outcome.why: The reply reported how useful, accurate and detailed the prompt audit was, citing its report.

parts.text: Look into whether prompts can be dissected sentence by sentence to verify each ask, possibly one prompt at a time with Haiku.

outcome.why: The prompt mastermind's brief covers sentence-by-sentence prompt dissection, with Haiku as a cheap first pass.

add.subject: sessions need to be creating tasks and projects, and every task logged to its session

parts.text: AIs must be able to create tasks inside sessions, which is the prime objective; take care creating tasks, getting them done, and wiring session completion to those tasks
System architect should review the session-to-task flow
A task created from a session gets logged to that session
Basic indexing like this should happen automatically
Fix both gaps: a tool used without proper indexing, and sessions not using the tool at all
Provide a task tool, possibly an item tool that creates a task
Owner is unsure what task tooling works now or what the tool is called
Sessions create tasks and projects, organize prompts into them, and get them done
Wire session completion to all its tasks and projects, and keep a reference to moved items so the session can still load them
Support nested tasks, where a subtask can act as a requirement
Might need a session mastermind
Quick tasks may auto-launch; unsure how many tasks spawn a subsession
When a mastermind deems a task worthy of a session, a session appears inside the session
Any session can have a child session
Child sessions must be indexed as properly as any other session
Nest child sessions inside the parent session directory rather than flattening them
Hand tasks off to the child session; system architect works out how the handoff happens
Open question: whether handed-off tasks auto-execute, get queued, or stay as manual loose ends

outcome.why: The prime objective is still being worked by the architect; the session-flow and prompt-tasks merges are partial steps.

parts.text: System architect is the generalist for the whole AI system, knows Servex and MCP, and handles item-system tooling; a session is an item

outcome.why: The AI system architect role readme names it the architect of the AI system, covering Servex, MCP and tooling.

parts.text: Objective: complete all tasks every day and as many as possible; write this down as the objective

outcome.why: priority.md opens with the written objective to complete as many tasks as possible every day.

parts.text: System architect's primary objectives: account for sessions properly, including nesting and data structure, and convert every prompt into tracked, logged, sound task data

outcome.why: The architect's role readme has a section listing its primary objectives (the owner, 2026-10-22).

parts.text: And then the tasks
Retroactively audit past sessions and prompts as session auditing, and fix the sessions
Owner doubts prior prompt audits were accurate, since agents lacked context and the work was not really done
Architect audits itself or spawns helpers: reread prompts, add missed subtasks, make sessions undeniably better, extract value, then mark complete
Session audits and prompt audits are similar
Do not create tasks just to check off work already documented or done
Attribute a paragraph to an outcome, file or change when it covers one topic; sentence-level is ideal
Unsure whether per-sentence processing is needed; maybe

add.subject: task resolution, AI system architect, tasks and sessions getting done

parts.text: Owner introduces the next idea, task resolution, and calls it important.
Define how tasks get completed in Node instead of hoping the AI remembers; retroactive audits are not enough; all sessions and all tasks should get resolved, so figure out the right way.
A task is a process that needs minimal Node processing so it gets either documented or done.
Who decides a task is done? If the minion working on it decides, one session ended up with 43 tasks, mostly noise.
Some tasks are obviously just done, checked off and complete; a simple quick fix is simply done.
Completion could combine percentage complete with confidence in the completion, so a task is done properly at a high confidence level.
A second agent reviewing a task is not the worst thing, but reviewers add little for quick fixes, so review is probably not required for simple tasks and most agents can just finish them.
Link tasks to their raw prompts so completing an accurate task completes its prompt; a separate completion class per prompt looks redundant; the round trip risks things falling through the cracks.
Round trip: a session holds prompts, prompts become tasks, and completing a task checks off its prompt; a session completes when all its prompts complete, and 100% coverage means the system works.
Agents often move on to the next task and may drift from the prescribed steps, which could be more flexible and useful; the agent may then revise its process.

outcome.why: resolution.md defines how tasks end in Node: evidence-backed completion, node chasing started tasks, and documenting caveats; the build list is still unticked.

parts.text: No noise: do not create tasks just to write things down; keep an eye on usage; not everything needs to be a task; these are basic operating principles.

outcome.why: resolution.md section 1 says noise is a failure and only an ask becomes a task, and the 44 noise tasks were stopped.

parts.text: Have the AI system architect optimize the task system and keep managing and improving it.
What needs to be a task, what shouldn't be, where should it go, and should it be handed off to a sub-agent?
How do we group tasks?
Group tasks into 3 to 5 tasks with subtasks instead of 43 flat tasks.
The AI system architect revises task descriptions to be short, sweet and concise, keeping just the right amount of wording to guide the system.
The AI system architect identifies problems with the system; that is the whole point.
Rename it the AI system architect, since it is primarily the architect of skills, roles, spawning, the SDK and tasks, not of fixing non-AI systems like items, pages, routing, data and streaming.

outcome.why: The AI system architect was given task optimisation as its top priority, and that work is an open task.

parts.text: We want to identify requirements; an easy way to add one is to make it a task, as something that needs to happen.

outcome.why: resolution.md section 3 makes a requirement a subtask, which adopts the owner's idea of making a requirement a task.

parts.text: Soft guidance is not a requirement; do not turn guidance into a requirement; put it in the task content as notes or bullets, phrased as suggestions.

outcome.why: resolution.md section 3 says a suggestion stays as a bullet in the task content and never blocks completion.

parts.text: Forcing guidance into an absolute rule makes the agent bend a square peg into a round hole; simplifying decisions would often be better in the long run.

outcome.why: resolution.md section 3 states that a guess turned into a hard rule makes agents force a square peg into a round hole.

parts.text: For any other module, use a module mastermind.

outcome.why: The architect's readme now leaves items, pages and streaming to module masterminds, and mastermind-item and mastermind-test were spawned.

parts.text: We still need to work out how the module masterminds work.

outcome.why: No doc or task shows how module masterminds work; the owner's note that this is still to be worked out has no follow-up in the record.

parts.text: The prompt should drive task creation for at least some tasks.
The AI can and probably should create generic overarching steps, a project or process that fills the gaps from the request to a solid plan.
Which process applies to building, reviewing and screenshotting, and which caveats go with which process?
Unsure whether task creation needs the process system; probably not, and the real question is what should be a task.

outcome.why: The live prompt splitter turns a prompt into one to three tasks, and resolution.md says a prompt makes 1-3 tasks.

parts.text: The masterminds make the decisions about what is a task, what isn't, where it goes, and whether it goes to a sub-agent.

outcome.why: resolution.md section 6 gives the parent mastermind the decision on leftover caveats, though what counts as a task is set by a rule table rather than the mastermind.

parts.text: Owner wraps up the thought.

add.subject: builders finishing tasks that might not be complete

parts.text: Builders should not routinely finish or mark a task complete when it might not actually be completed.

outcome.why: resolution.md section 6 requires evidence for complete and says a worker cannot mark a task complete on its own say-so.

parts.text: Can the agents properly assess the completion state?

outcome.why: The reply says a worker cannot mark a task complete on its own say-so and completion needs evidence, answering whether agents can judge completion.

parts.text: Improve task creation and completion so agents do not mark tasks complete on hallucinated or guessed assessments, even though the AI is not always perfect and we are not fully convinced.

outcome.why: Some creation and completion fixes are merged, but the build list in resolution.md, including refusing complete without evidence, is still open.

parts.text: For the system architect: run a risk analysis of where things might fall through the cracks and where the systems set up may not be working adequately.

outcome.why: cracks.md is a measured risk analysis of where tasks fall through the cracks, with counts and the check for each.

parts.text: If a requested item is not going to be done, document it.

outcome.why: resolution.md section 6 says anything asked but not done is written down as a loose end rather than dropped.

parts.text: Document such loose ends in an existing markdown note that references the task or file, saying the item was requested but not done, and why.

outcome.why: resolution.md says a loose end is a line in the module readme, linked to the task, matching the owner's note-plus-reference request.

parts.text: For tasks that are not 100% clear, should the extra mentioned things that were not done be done anyway?

outcome.why: The reply says leftovers go to the mastermind as caveats to decide, answering whether extra items should be done.

parts.text: The mastermind might be the one who makes that decision.

outcome.why: resolution.md section 6 has the parent mastermind decide each caveat: do it, take a quick stab, or write it as a loose end.

parts.text: Taking a quick first stab at something may be a strategy to see if it is worth doing; if that doesn't work out, the owner doesn't know what then.

outcome.why: resolution.md section 6 lists 'take a quick stab' as one of the three options for a caveat.

parts.text: What is the resolution of the tasks?

outcome.why: The reply sets out how tasks resolve: evidence plus confidence, documented leftovers, and node chasing started tasks.

parts.text: Once the AI starts finishing tasks, this may be a source of problems we have to address.

outcome.why: cracks.md row 3 measures completion claims with no proof (42 of 92 reached complete), the problem the owner anticipated.

parts.text: Shouldn't Node be involved in monitoring tasks once they are completed?

outcome.why: The reply says node watches started tasks and red-flags blocked or silent ones, answering whether node should monitor tasks.

parts.text: Completion is probably already automatic from session completion data: if the server or a client loads the session and its log, it knows whether the session is completed.

outcome.why: resolution.md section 4 says a session is complete when its prompts and tasks are, computed rather than marked by hand.

parts.text: Should the Node server managing the SDKs register each new task with itself and manually update its progress?

outcome.why: The reply says node watches started tasks and extends the existing TaskLoop and Heartbeat rather than building a second chaser.

parts.text: A task that doesn't update its progress within 10 or 15 minutes, especially an active one, could be flagged; dormant planning or suggested tasks that are never accepted are fine and need not be reprompted.

outcome.why: resolution.md section 8 chases started tasks after about 5 minutes and leaves proposed and accepted tasks alone, as the owner suggested.

parts.text: Don't rely on the AI remembering to close out a task.

outcome.why: resolution.md opens by stating that a task should not end on the agent remembering, and node chases started tasks instead.

parts.text: If a task was created but not updated or closed, Node reprompts with the number of open tasks and asks for an update.
If the AI says it already finished the task, it closes the task, and we figure out why it wasn't able to follow the instructions.

outcome.why: Node chases started tasks for status, but the reprompt with a count of open tasks is not in the doc and the chase is still an unticked build item.

parts.text: Maybe we need a start-task skill or tool, since a task can be accepted as worth doing and ready to start before it is actually started.

outcome.why: resolution.md section 5 adds a started state that an agent enters by its own start call, separate from accepted, though the tool is not built.

parts.text: That is an important distinction.
The mastermind creates the task but does not start it; it hands the task off to a minion who starts it, whether it is queued and not awaiting approval or handled some other way.

outcome.why: resolution.md section 5 separates accepted (queued, nobody on it) from started (an agent on it now), matching the owner's hand-off model.

parts.text: Add a started-task tool that tells the system a task has been started, meaning an agent is currently working on that specific task, in flight.

outcome.why: A start tool is only on resolution.md's unticked build list, so the architect's open task carries the build.

parts.text: If a started task does not finish within a timeout, the agent working on it gets reprompted.
Example reprompt: 'Hey, it's been a minute, can we get a status update?'
The timeout might be 5 minutes.

outcome.why: resolution.md section 8 reprompts a started task that goes quiet for about 5 minutes, with a red flag after repeated silence.

parts.text: Once started, every task needs to be finished as soon as possible; we keep an eye on it and either it gets finished or it gets red-flagged if blocked.

outcome.why: resolution.md section 8 says a blocked or silent started task gets a red flag on the board.

parts.text: That is the right picture.
In that sense, Node is involved in reprompting for updates on tasks.

outcome.why: resolution.md section 8 has node chase started tasks for status, which is the reprompting role the owner described.

parts.text: With session data, task data, and completion data all wired up properly, we should get a very clear picture of what happens for each session.
The owner should be able to click through the sessions and see the whole breakdown for each one.

outcome.why: The commit backfills 805 parent links between task and child-session folders, wiring the session, task and child data together, though the full click-through view is not verified.

parts.text: Yeah.

parts.text: The owner stresses that the system prompt versus conversation distinction, and how compaction interacts with it, is very important.

Make the role system survive auto compaction: either add our own compaction hook, skill, or tool that re-injects our system prompt, or append to the system prompt the proper SDK way so it is not compacted and summarized away.
Without re-injection the system prompt is almost guaranteed to be less effective, drifts after hundreds of thousands of tokens, and is not freshened.
Readme layout is up to the AI; the role system surviving compaction is important.
Create framework/AI files for context drift and compaction, including auto compaction caveats, cross-referencing each other.
We already have notes about context drift.
Each file identifies specific ideas and keeps a thorough yet minimal list of complicating factors; which file holds what does not matter.
The context drift file mentions compaction and the compaction file mentions context drift, each with a short general summary of the other and how it applies.
Filler: the owner is unsure about the readme details.
The owner is reading through roles.js.
What is a Cervex role, and is the Cervex roles system (roles row and roles.js) object-oriented?
Lean into object-oriented design wherever necessary.
Upgrade the non-object-oriented Cervex roles system to object-oriented, and work out how roles are organized, referenced, and used.
A session has a role, and sessions.jsonl records exactly which role was used.
Show all the properties of a role.
Any session can be tagged with a specific role.
Look into the role system OO upgrade; it is not top priority, so work on it when tokens allow.
Create a task queue that prioritizes work by estimated cost, priority, importance, and potential outcome.
Also raise priority for things the owner keeps asking for that were supposed to be done but were never finished.
If a task queue already exists, make it object-oriented.
Link the owner to the task queue so they can watch how it works in real time.
Show how the queue integrates with sessions, tasks, Cervex, how agents are spawned, and how tasks are queued.
Show, don't tell: when the owner asks how something works, demonstrate it on screen rather than explaining it.
Build views so the owner can see object-oriented structures, classes, instances, properties, and data structures in real time.
Write down the object-oriented system for the entire project.
Anything the project does creates objects; objects have classes, and we create instances of them.
Instances are visible on screen with their properties and data structures, so during a demo the owner can see the actual data structures as the program runs.
The owner says this is super important for pretty much everything.

parts.text: Owner just heard of framework/AI/merge; a card there is a duplicate being set aside.
Is there something there to look at or not?
Page mastermind: look at the different ways pages are created, focusing on navigation.
Page masterminds plan.
Readme pages could be linked to properly; maybe that is the simplest way.
How is linked markdown rendered: does it keep the parent page's navigation or get swapped out?
Pages with their own persistent navigation (top or left tabs) swap a content area; pages without their own navigation should swap out the parent.
Many pages go Miller-column style, deeper and deeper; the Miller column idea is liked but never solidified and is always a little broken.
What size is each column?

Column sizing options: a row capped at comfortable reading width (800 to 1000 px) within 3000 px available; clicking a card either opens another capped row (managing space) or splits the space into two 1500-plus px columns, which stretches things too big.
Having the page mastermind work from a plan is not bad.
Prioritize the page system: have the page mastermind look into how items, pages, data and streaming interact, and build a rock-solid page, data and streaming system.
Items are like sub-pages; pages are items, each with a page.jsonl that streams, and any item saves into that page.jsonl unless it uses its own file or subdirectory.
A separate file or subdirectory used by an item must be noted in the root page.jsonl.
The item tool can be the page tool; no separate page tool is needed because pages are items.
How does the item tool instantiate items and apply deltas server side (MCP or system tool), and has that been built and tested? It is not clear how what we've built works.
Any AI or UI should be able to use these tools to manipulate pages and items through standard delta form.
Check that all of this is documented properly so the page mastermind knows what we are doing and trying to do.
We need automated tests for the core systems: page, item, data, persistence and streaming.
Was the rudimentary testing system asked for yesterday built? Maybe it was.
Run tests at the right time, not too often; do not bog down the machine with many worktrees each running a dev server and tests on every file change.
It should happen automatically: when a new worktree starts or files change, a monitor loads pages to catch syntax errors, reports them, and runs the tests.
Agents should not have to remember to run tests.
Possibly run only the tests tied to a changed file, or retest dependent classes; that shape seems right, though unsure it is possible.
Report failures back to the builder and/or mastermind so they can put out fires as quickly as possible.
Page mastermind should lean into the testing system and lock down processes for items and pages; unsure where the testing system is at.

add.subject: task queue that survives sessions

parts.text: Build a prioritized task queue for each mastermind that survives session boundaries.
Look at past work first, since there have been task queues before.
Support dynamic reprioritization across the whole board when tokens run short and we enter token crunch mode.

The mastermind autonomously monitors its own task queue, prioritizes, fixes and improves, getting the most important and easiest work done first, and gives specific requests priority based on token usage.
Each mastermind has its own prioritized task queue.
The queue persists past the session barrier, so a fresh session picks it up.
Store tasks per session in tasks.jsonl alongside session.jsonl, not per day or month; the daily or monthly idea is superseded.
Have the page mastermind or system architect work out the best architecture and data structure for the jsonl streaming system.
Add a planning stage where masterminds identify the most important projects, investigate, and propose a plan, with the owner refining it or approving before launch, and decide what gets done first.
Planning can waste time and money, since the AI is often just as good at doing the task directly.
Triage by size: quick fixes are just done without planning, medium fixes are the mastermind's judgment call on whether to plan, and large projects get planned.
Major architectural decisions must be planned, especially ones that affect all future APIs and data structures, so the right design is chosen.
Don't put things in the wrong files or places, don't use the wrong API, and never recreate streaming logic or data storage.
Create a robust item system that streams properly, can save anywhere and load, and supports everything we need.

parts.text: Make sure agents use the task system properly by setting the framework for what needs a task and when.
If the parent task's scope covers the work, just do it; no child task is needed for everything.
If the work is unrelated to the parent task, make a sibling or child task so token consumption is attributed to what was actually done.
If there is a plan, pre-create the tasks before they happen.
Agents should always use the task system, possibly through Node, even when no tasks are specified.
Any agent given a prompt creates its task first; if it has no official task to work on, it needs one.
Spawned agents should arrive with a pre-created task handed off, so the mastermind and the agent both link to it and use the item tool to read and update it.
Only the sub agent updates a handed-off task; roles must be clear so two agents never modify the same task in conflicting ways.
Once the mastermind hands off a task, it belongs to the builder or agent until it is done.
When the task passes back, that could trigger a review process.
The task management system is a complex problem.
Often the AI runs in autonomous mode without a plan, deciding what to do next.
A single task may need breaking into many smaller parts.
Tasks may involve a lot of investigation and discovery.
Document investigation in tasks: record decisions and key findings as quick notes, then move on to the next thing.
The documentation need not be only tasks; it could be arbitrary content or notes.
Tasks could easily have notes built in.
How should tasks and notes appear in the chronological chat log, given that tasks are saved separately?
The log could hold references to tasks and notes, and if it loads chronologically it could render a time-based replay of tasks being worked on and notes being created.
Not sure how arbitrary content cards get added to tasks or sessions.
Make session extend task, so it has the same completion logic.
Do it properly: spawn an agent, or use a mastermind if we have one, to manage the process.
Transition properly from the current state to the new state.
Write automated tests so that manipulating tasks and sessions does not break things.
The architect was asked to devise a test system; check whether it was built, and if not, build it.
Don't overwrite too many tests.
Keep tests performant: don't bog down the computer, run too many tests, or spend too much time writing them.
We looked into testing before.
Acknowledgement.
The agent is able to add tasks.
Servex replays the folder's log, is that right?
Instantiating tasks or sessions server-side is okay as long as it works properly.
Concern: client, Servex, server, and file system state could diverge, with potentially four locations to keep synchronized.
Parent references can be by session ID or by path, but they must be consistent.
Writes to big records take more than 60 seconds; why would that be?
What do you mean by writes to big records?
Shouldn't it not matter how big the JSON-L file is?
We're doing append-only writes, right?

parts.text: Give a quick overview of the test system: what the file pattern is, and whether tests go in the core test folder or are localized to each class.
Tests belong in their own class folder. Node-compatible tests are named ClassName.node.tests.js and create new test instances.
Build automated tests for all the classes and figure out the most useful ones.
For object-oriented classes, most tests instantiate the object and check that it was set up properly.
Layer the tests, with a basic test as the first layer.
The basic test makes one instance and runs about 15 method calls, checking results at each stage. It is the quick run that shows nothing has broken.
The basic test should catch about 99% of errors.
Run the tests automatically in real time, rerunning whenever anything changes. Only report failures, not passes.
Deliver real-time test failures to the builder, the agent writing the code, since it can fix them most easily. The mastermind may also get them.
Interim errors during multi-file writes, such as a page breaking before both files land, are not urgent enough to notify immediately.
Awareness of interim errors could guide when a rerun happens.
Will constant error feedback pollute the agent's context, given that agents generally shouldn't be breaking things?
Agents should not produce console errors or thrown JavaScript errors. Any such error means they broke something, and they should be able to create and edit files without throwing errors.
The owner is unsure the no-errors rule is right and may be wrong about it.

"Probably better" to call it an AI architect, and it "maybe" lives in the framework AI directory rather than the Cervex directory.
Unsure where the Cervex mastermind file lives for that role.
The AI system is more overarching than Cervex, though there is "a fair amount of stuff on the Cervex" in the SDK.
There could be multiple homes for documentation; corrected: "Not the data structures."

The mastermind reads the necessary READMEs, which should be as up to date as the last mastermind; keep things as documented as possible per prompt.
Do not log every single thing separately; "That wasn't the right." Logging belongs in the raw session log file, and our own session log is fine for the big core things.

add.subject: use an item tool to check the session's completion

parts.text: For any session, use an item tool to check the session's completion.
Ideally a quick response that tallies the current state of all the session's tasks; 'I don't know how quickly with our current system'.
Run that completion check on all past sessions and refine and review them to a completion state; 'We don't need to do that audit yet, but that's the idea, right?'

Don't keep important information in session.jsonl that belongs elsewhere (re 'closeout.md' and 'the real record is batched right into session.jsonl'). The session can reference it, but conclusive information about a module can't be buried in session.jsonl. We don't want things lost in the session; when we can, write to documentation, which is often the preferred way.
Anecdotal notes ('here's what was done' and 'what's still in the plan') probably belong outside the session, 'for some projects anyway'; owner is 'still trying to sort this out'.

A closeout could be a message or markdown entry written to session.jsonl, a conclusion answering 'did we finish properly?' and 'what's the state of the thing?'; it 'probably should be, yeah, definitely more structured'.
Keep the document in module documentation where it belongs ('not sure how I feel about that' about closeout); the session can reference that file, e.g. when it's added to a specific task.
Treat the session log like the console log's grouping: starting a task could route all following logs to that task, or the task could be started and logs written directly to its path.
We don't 'necessarily' need to log everything into the raw session log; a high-level overview in the session log is often useful, and purely ephemeral, session-only material belongs there.
The session should be able to add notes or cards to any substructure, per subtask or prompt and not just per session; 'I don't think we have that yet'.
Get the live transcribe working again so web transcribe can be used instead of this app; it is 'wonky and broken'.
Someone should take a look at how the chat bubbles are created and how the deltas are applied; it is 'not very robust, or at least' 'glitchy'.
'Not sure how we're doing on usage.'
Owner is scrolling through the file; 'so the file isn't the problem'.
What does the agent mean by 'scanning the 3 megabyte list of every agent ever started and adds up every task's cost every time from scratch'?
'Sounds like' that is a batch calculation that runs on every single task.
If a task or session hasn't been updated since it was last computed, don't compute it again.
'Every task's cost' may be the old system where sessions were mislabeled as tasks; 'I don't think that's necessary unless' it uses the task index to find child tasks.
A child session should be embedded in the parent session.

'I don't understand why' after each append the item tool rebuilds the whole session picture from outside sources; we don't need to recompute all sessions when one updates, just update the one session that changed ('Just update the one session that changed, right?'), since its raw log is likely more current with more changes and cost.
'So that makes, you know, sense'; 'I don't know why that seems obvious'.
The current behavior 'maybe' is just how the script was originally written.
The session's own file should already name its children; 'I don't know why it wouldn't be'.

When any session spawns an agent with the SDK tool, the new session should be programmatically added to the parent session.jsonl as a task (prompts and quick-fix tasks can be tasks too, and so can a session), so the parent's completion depends on the child's completion; 'If that's not already working that way, it should be... So make sure that happens.'
'Me asking to make sure that happens... shouldn't have to say that.'
Make a task to track the completion of what was just asked for.

Sculpt the potential shape of the solution early, and add that to the refinement step run by Haiku or Sonnet ('I don't know if we can'), defining what completion looks like: 'Have we properly completed this task?'
This is part of the process for tasks of substance, not necessarily every quick-fix task.
Scope varies greatly; finding the quick, easiest solutions, proposing them, and weighing them against moderate-to-heavy complexity, better features, and long-term robustness is part of the AI's job.
'That could be upgraded' from a task to a project.
'I don't know if there's anything in our skill system' for choosing between a simple task, a quick task, or no task.
Some file-tool work doesn't actually need a task; if it applies directly to the parent task, scope-wise, just do it.

We want work attributed to the right task: don't sit in the wrong task logging and spending tokens because the last task wasn't closed out; creating and finishing tasks appropriately needs careful attention.
'I'm not sure the best way to actually make sure that happens'?
Starting a task is a delta: the item tool starts the task and the same item tool finishes it.
Finishing one task in a series could prompt the next, e.g. finishing step three automatically injects step four's instructions.
Where did the process system land, including chained task prompting? 'I remember asking for it' and 'I'm not sure I've seen a single thing regarding it.'
'Hopefully' the things being built can be seen in an object-oriented browser view showing class structure, properties, and API, demoed in real time.
'I don't know if we have a role' or roles for VS Code sidebar instances.
'We might want one', with something in it about the prompt refinement hook.

Each new VS Code sidebar, especially one identified as a VS Code sidebar mastermind ('if I had identified as'), should know the prompt refinement hook and how it works, and should read the refinement file after each prompt, going sentence by sentence through the raw prompts and comparing them to the produced task to make sure there's no mistake and to embellish certain parts.
'If there's certain' parts, the hook 'is going to do a quick rough version'.
The agent can fix any part of the refinement ('frankly, you can fix any part of it').
Judge the name of each of the tasks.
'We're trying to create a very clear picture of what I'm asking for.'
When the prompt refinement comes in, quickly via Haiku, it should render instantly to the session detail page; 'Make sure, here, let me click over and do that right now'.
'I haven't checked a session detail page in a while.'

add.subject: EB0F session lookup, session ID switching and log misattribution, session folder and spawn paths, cost tracking, mastermind context rollover

parts.text: How does the owner find "this" (the EB0F session) on the sessions list?
Look into what the "EB0F" session is.
Is "resumed from" a reference to our own session log?
Owner says the session logging gets really confusing.
When a session is mysteriously switched to a new session ID, all the session log stuff "probably goes to a new point".
How are session folders created (per day, named from the role) and how is session.jsonl placed in them?
How is a spawned session recorded, in the session that is spawned to do the work?
VS Code sidebar creates its own session, and each SDK automatically gets one, the owner thinks.
Does the spawn tool specify the working path or name for a session, and how is availability of that path name in the namespace checked?
How is an SDK session ID switch handled, where the session appears to fork itself?
Track the session ID switch; the owner says "we want to track it" and that session ID switching is "important to track".
Track costs properly and accurately ("We need to track the costs properly", "We want to track it accurately").
Look into how our system works and figure out the two mysteries (the EB0F session and the session ID switch).
Thoroughly document the whole problem and solution space in its own file, and make sure it is noted somewhere and indexed.
The session system must not misattribute things, lose data, put data in the wrong place, double-account, or fail to account for anything. This is "of absolute importance".
Not sure if there is any way to identify the session.
Could we enforce that one specific session ID is the only one allowed to write to session.jsonl? "Maybe that's the thing."
Maybe it is permission-based ("you're not the agent"), though that would stop an agent from adding a log to a different session's file.
Not sure what the key is, but "one way to do it, at least for SDK sessions that we have the ID of", is to map each SDK session to its directory.
Not sure whether to limit who can write to the session log.
Explore the consequences of an agent using the wrong session log: it would be "disastrous", and wrong content in the wrong place could be hard to reverse if it is unclear who did it and why.
Is it possible that when the AI system mastermind was revived it came back with a new session ID?
Owner is working through the question ("I don't know why that would, well, okay").
Long-lived roles "should be getting new session IDs" sometimes, because they are reset.
"Resumed from" might just be a reference to the last session, with a new session created each day so it does not get too big.
Rolling over to a new session is dangerous: do not switch sessions mid-flight on something, or work is lost and loose ends never get finished.
The owner says the rollover is "a unique context".
The AI system mastermind is supposed to roll over to a new session periodically.
Add "like a timeout" for the AI system mastermind ("we want like a timeout for it").
Unsure whether reuse should depend on a timeout or on the topic.
Reuse one with the same context for a follow-up question 15 to 30 minutes later ("we could reuse the same one").
If the question is a completely different topic and the mastermind has a bloated context, "we should just start from scratch".
Maybe lean into a dynamic session that any mastermind can use, managing its context, rather than a single reusable mastermind; "I think that should be built into the mastermind system".

Any mastermind spawning agents should track what goes into its context, its maximum context window, the current percentage used and how long it has run, and recycle, renew or compact at appropriate times, so compaction does not happen while it is working on something.
A mastermind reusing a past session that has run too long could "potentially" trigger compaction with the /compact command first.
After triggering compaction, the mastermind should wait for it to finish.
How would the mastermind actually listen for compaction finishing?
Never wait on something that never finishes or never sends a notification, because the whole process would stop.
Owner says these are all questions they are not sure about.

parts.text: How is the sessions preview grid being queried right now?
Default the sessions preview to a limited view, “either the last month or day”, instead of loading everything.
Use a sessions index file per year, month and day so only those items load; owner says this “shouldn't be hard”.
Each parent session may be a VS Code sidebar mastermind that spawned sub-masterminds and minions, so one parent can hold hundreds of subsessions, which makes loading everything heavy.

Add load thresholds: a preview may not need everything, but a proper total cost may need all tasks and subtasks loaded. Owner does not know the current indexing and load order (“we kind of need these load thresholds”).

Alternative: the preview shows only own cost, and total cost is reached by clicking through to the session. Owner finds this limiting, since it hides data they “should probably be able to see”, and is unsure.
Look into the dynamic query system, or whether the server loads all sessions and can query them by looping; owner recalls asking for this at one point.
Server side, in a cached way, compute all session costs, “maybe even in real time”.
Keep instances of all sessions in memory; as new messages come in and costs are recalculated, update them so the grid renders properly.
Where does the dynamic server-side query work stand?
On the session detail page, are the listed tasks actually counted? Are they all proposed tasks, and do the play and stop buttons mean anything, or is it a UI artifact not yet wired up?
The task list UI needs enhancing: the task text seems “truncated or highly summarized”, and a narrow column wraps it to 3 to 6 lines instead of a full-width sentence.
The session detail page should show its tasks in a data grid with filters, the same UI as the sessions page, so the owner can filter the tasks.
For a long-running session, sorting the tasks by day could be useful.
Before the session detail work, first get the sessions page rendering something more useful.
Are the tasks showing on the sessions page the Haiku-generated tasks?
Verify the system is tailing sessions as tasks come in, “making sure they get refined into actual useful outcomes”, then checked off and completed.
How sure are we that all these tasks are tracked and organized properly, given 51 of 90 completed? Owner says the whole experience still doesn't work terribly well.
Get web dictation working on the website so the owner can dictate directly to an agent there, rather than switching back to this app. Owner says this would be ideal.
Owner is not sure we are there yet; the dictation system seemed very buggy and broken.

Find out whether there is a “quick way” to wire the website dictation into this tab, using the website microphone instead of this app's, with transcription and prompt refinement working as similarly to this one as possible.
Check whether the transcription can be appended to this VS Code sidebar session, or whether a message can be sent to it. Owner is unsure: “I think maybe there's not a way to do that.”
Find a way to carry on this transcription via the website dictation. Owner is unsure whether that would be easy.
How is the dictation setup currently wired?

Subsessions are also just added to the tasks

Any subsession, prompt, or task "automatically just gets scheduled for completion" and gets tracked
"I like that shape."

add.subject: Servex restart session ID, task folders vs. parent session, tracking child sessions and subsessions, moving tasks between chats and sessions

parts.text: Make sure that restarting the Servex does not fork the session ID.

A new session ID for the system mastermind is 'acceptable' (owner recalls agent saying so), but 'however' the role must be 'ultra clear' that everything is always logged properly, because it can restart at any time, so no elaborate handoff process. Always keep the documentation for that role in the framework AI readme system.

'Maybe' a framework AI system.md so the system mastermind knows its roles, capabilities and operating procedures. Any directory could be an AI system with its README and multiple roles, e.g. a mastermind.md loaded only for an actual mastermind, giving per-directory roles. 'I guess that's not really important right now.'
'Let's just try and stay focused.' Reading what is in this session's record.
What does the breakdown mean: 241 tasks created by prompt refinement, 28 by a backfill of older prompts, 15 by agents? What exactly are the 15 by agents?
Does each task get its own folder, or are they just tasks within the parent session?
Why are they not organized? '241 or 284, or however many, that's a lot of tasks.'
Prompt refinement should create not only the individual tasks that need tracking and completion, but also a parent task grouping a handful of subtasks 'when appropriate'.
How many root-level tasks are there?
Child sessions are not entries in the task list. There are 17 task folder link lines, while 46 task folders sit on disk under the session. What are the 17 link lines as opposed to the 46 folders?

Any task can define its own folder with its own task.jsonl as a breakout, but 'I think the default should be' that creating a task in a session just adds it to the parent session.jsonl, so it needs no folder by default.
'I think maybe' a project was defined as a task that needs its own folder and can be moved around more freely, but needs to be indexed by the parent.
Track child sessions (and subsessions) properly, for accounting, rendering and organization. 'I've asked for that a dozen times.' 'Obviously we want to track them.'
Child sessions should be able to have their own tasks, 'right?'
We need a way to create child sessions and pass tasks from the parent session.
When a session is created to handle a designed task or project, the handoff 'shouldn't be' a chat message. It should be 'here's your task folder'.
A sub session needs its own directory, I think, with its own session.jsonl and the ability to have folders within it.
Creating a sub session for a specific task, and treating a subsession as a task, is 'sort of an acceptable thing'.

A task could be upgraded to a session: its title, requirements and prompt carry over into a session in its own folder. 'It could look very similar'; in the UI the prompt turns into a task, and the task becomes a session. The upgrade happens 'as the agent deems it necessary'.
Once an agent spawns, the subsession has its own cost management and can spawn its own subsessions.
What are we thinking on tracking child sessions?

The spawn agent SDK tool does the subsession. The parent session.jsonl needs a record that it spawned a subsession, with all configuration (a reference to the subsession, its model ID, role, other parameters and system prompts). 'We want as much data as possible about the things that we're making.'
'We need to be writing the shit down.' Tools should document what they are doing so everything can be reviewed.
When creating tasks and upgrading them to sessions, the relevant tasks should go into that session.
As in the chat view, when a past item is moved into a newly created session, does it disappear from its chronological place in the chat?

'I don't think so. Although it could.' The moved item could be dimmed, with an arrow and overlay icon noting it was moved; clicking the link scrolls down to where it went. 'That actually feels like a pretty cool UX,' but it has never been seen and 'could be tricky to get working properly'.

This avoids constantly duplicating a view of something that exists elsewhere, which confuses users ('what is this new thing we're creating?'). On the card in its new home, an incoming-arrow icon overlaid on the top-left corner says it was moved in from the parent chat.
Give an overview of where we're at on these things and what we should be doing here.
